changes.before: Use mapped and conditional types so each event name carries its matching payload.
changes.after: Keep each event name paired with the right details.

before: An event is a value describing something that happened. Its type field names the event, and its payload holds that event's details. One event might carry a title; another might carry a percentage. A useful type keeps the name paired with the correct details. Merely allowing either name and either payload independently would allow incorrect combinations.

K extends keyof Details means K must be one of those allowed keys. A conditional type has the form condition ? typeIfTrue : typeIfFalse. never describes an impossible type with no valid values. In PayloadFor<K>, the valid key selects Details[K]. Because K is already constrained to keyof Details, the condition is always satisfied for allowed uses; it still shows the conditional-type syntax.

Read the mapped type in stages. [K in keyof Details] visits each key while building a type. At selected it builds {type: 'selected'; payload: {label: string}}. At counted it builds the matching count shape. The final [keyof Details] takes the built property types and combines them into a union. Each union member still contains its correctly paired name and payload.

Checking event.type === 'selected' narrows DemoEvent to its selected member, so event.payload.label is known to exist there. In the remaining branch, counted's count is available. Trying a selected event with only count fails the compiler. You can understand or expand the mapped declaration into two explicit union members; the reusable form is useful when the key list grows.

The exercise calls its map Payloads, with opened/title and progress/percent. The starter supplies those type declarations. Keep their public names, trace how AppEvent connects each name to its payload, and format the opened and progress sentences exactly. The % in a template string is ordinary displayed punctuation after the percentage; it is not an arithmetic remainder operator there. The mapping preserves relationships, not where an event came from at runtime.

Temporarily pair opened with {percent: 50} and run the full TypeScript check to see a rejection, then remove the invalid call. Types are erased at runtime, so real incoming events still require validation. An event with a numeric percent also needs a separate range rule if you intend to require 0 through 100; the current type number alone does not impose that rule.
after: An event describes something that happened. Its type property names the event. Its payload is the data about that event. Each name needs the right kind of payload.
The example has selected events with a text label, and counted events with a number. Keyof gets the allowed event names. A type lookup gets the details for one name.
PayloadFor uses a type parameter K for an allowed name. The conditional type chooses the matching details. Never means no value is allowed; here, K is already limited to valid names.
The mapped type builds one event shape for each key. The final `[keyof Details]` combines those shapes into a union. Each shape keeps its own name and payload together. No loop runs to do this.
Checking event.type identifies the event shape. The selected path can read label. The counted path can read count. Mixing a selected name with a count-only payload causes a type error.

The project uses opened with a title, and progress with a percent. Return Opened Notes for the supplied opened event and Progress 50% for the supplied progress event. The percent sign is ordinary text here.
Types check your code before it runs. Incoming events still need real value checks. A number type also does not limit percent to the range 0 through 100.

before: Describe the data each event carries: opened has a title, and progress has a percent. This data is called its payload.
For each event name, build a type with type and payload fields. Keep each name paired with its matching data.
For opened with title "Notes", return "Opened Notes".
after: Keep opened paired with a text title and progress paired with a numeric percent.
Check event.type before reading its payload.
Return the requested sentence for each event.

before: The mapped type loops over `keyof Payloads`.
Each member should have `type: K` and `payload: Payloads[K]`.
Narrow using `event.type`, then read only the field for that case.
after: The mapped type builds a shape for each key in Payloads.
Each shape pairs `type: K` with `payload: Payloads[K]`.
Read title only for opened and percent only for progress.

before.question: AppEvent pairs opened with {title: string} and progress with {percent: number}. Which value keeps the progress event paired with its required payload?
before.explanation: The mapped union preserves each event name and its matching payload together. progress needs a numeric percent; title belongs to opened. A field that is valid for one event is not automatically valid for the other.

after.question: Which value correctly pairs progress with its details?
after.explanation: A progress event needs a numeric percent. A title belongs to an opened event.

changes.before: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: handle({ type: "opened", payload: { percent: 50 } }); The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.
changes.after: To try a type error, temporarily pair opened with a percent-only payload. Read the error, then restore a title payload.

project.title: A safe event system
project.task: Use the supplied paired event types and return the correct opened or progress message.
project.done_when: Valid pairs produce the requested text, mismatched pairs are rejected, and the checks pass.
